name: Receive ambulance patients and transfer care
summary: When paramedics bring a patient to the emergency department, the hospital must take the patient off the ambulance stretcher and accept responsibility before the crew can return to 911 calls. A triage nurse takes a verbal handover and assigns a CTAS level, a clerk opens the visit and the charge nurse looks for a free stretcher and nurse. When none is free, the patient waits in the hallway on the paramedics' stretcher with the crew, which is the offload delay that paramedic services and the province track. A dedicated offload nurse, where funded, can take several waiting patients and release crews early.

baseline.org_archetype: A three-site Ontario community hospital corporation with about 160,000 ED visits a year, one ambulance triage desk per site and partial Dedicated Offload Nurse Program coverage at the busiest site.
baseline.notes: Times describe the large site, where most ambulances go; the small sites have shorter queues but fewer spaces. 2020-2022 adds infection screening and fewer spaces per patient because of isolation needs.

trigger: A paramedic crew arrives at the ambulance bay with a patient (a pre-arrival patch for critical patients).
end_state: The receiving nurse has accepted care and signed the call report, the patient is on a hospital stretcher, in the offload area or in the waiting room, and the crew has cleared the hospital.

volume.seasonality: Busier in winter with respiratory viruses and on Mondays and late mornings to evenings; fewest arrivals overnight. Volume fell by about a fifth in 2020/21 with the pandemic.

evidence.note: 20% of Ontario ED visits arrived by ambulance in 2022/23 (OAG 2023) applied to the corporation's 126,357-161,049 ED visits a year (annual reports), divided by 12. The organisation file's 2,800 a month implies about 21-26% by ambulance.

surge.cause: Winter respiratory virus season (influenza and RSV; COVID-19 waves from 2020)

evidence.note: Taken from the organisation file's process map entry (author's estimate of the usual December-March rise in Ontario ED visits); no period source was opened that quantifies it.

systems.name: Hospital information system (electronic patient record with ADT, order entry, results, eMAR and clinical documentation)
Electronic bed board and patient flow dashboard
Email, telephone, pagers and wireless phones
Paramedic service electronic patient care record (ambulance call report)

resources.name: Emergency treatment spaces, large site (stretchers, chairs and resuscitation bays)
Staffed ambulance with a two-paramedic crew (regional paramedic service)

steps.name: Paramedics bring patient into the emergency department
steps.description: The two-person paramedic crew parks in the ambulance bay, unloads the patient on the ambulance stretcher and wheels them to the ambulance triage desk. They note the hospital arrival time in their electronic patient care record, which starts the offload clock the region tracks.

next.condition: patched ahead as critical (CTAS 1, trauma, stroke or STEMI pre-alert)

evidence.note: Author's general knowledge of Ontario ambulance arrival practice; arrival time is the start of the offload interval.

steps.name: Direct critical patient to resuscitation bay
steps.description: The charge nurse, who took the paramedic patch call through the switchboard before arrival, meets the crew at the door, confirms the resuscitation bay is ready and the emergency physician has been called, and waves the stretcher straight through without stopping at triage.

evidence.note: Author's general knowledge: patched CTAS 1 patients bypass the triage queue; CTAS 1 patients are seen immediately (ctas2016) but the bypass routine is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Resuscitation team takes bedside handover
steps.description: Three emergency nurses take the paramedics' verbal report at the resuscitation stretcher, slide the patient across, attach the monitor and start the resuscitation while the physician listens to the same report. The paramedics stay until the patient is moved and their equipment is removed.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of a resuscitation handover with a three-nurse team.

steps.name: Take verbal handover at ambulance triage
steps.description: The ambulance triage nurse finishes the patient in front, then listens to the paramedic's structured report: complaint, history, vital signs, treatment given, medications and allergies. The nurse reads the paper or printed call report summary and asks questions to fill gaps.

error.defect_description: Medication list, allergy or time of symptom onset not passed on or not written down.

evidence.note: OAG 2023 says all arrivals are assessed the same way and ambulance patients do not get priority over walk-ins; the queue length and handover time are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Assign a CTAS triage level
steps.description: The nurse picks the presenting complaint in eCTAS in the hospital system, enters the paramedic's vital signs and pain score plus a quick check of their own, and accepts or overrides the suggested Canadian Triage and Acuity Scale level from 1 to 5. The level sets the patient's priority for a stretcher and a physician.

error.defect_description: Triage level too low or too high; OAG 2023 reports eCTAS override rates of 14-16% a year, showing frequent nurse-system disagreement.

control.basis: Canadian Triage and Acuity Scale level recorded for every ED visit and reported to CIHI's National Ambulatory Care Reporting System; eCTAS promoted by Ontario Health

evidence.note: Triage by CTAS with eCTAS described in OAG 2023 (section 4.4); first-order modifiers are vital signs, pain and mechanism (ctas2016). Minutes are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Screen for infection risk and set precautions
steps.description: The nurse asks the screening questions for fever, cough and exposure and checks the paramedic's screening result. A positive screen means droplet and contact precautions and a single room or curtained space, which narrows the spaces the patient can go to. From 2020 to 2022 this followed the provincial COVID-19 screening rules.

control.basis: Hospital infection prevention and control policy (routine practices and additional precautions); provincial COVID-19 screening guidance 2020-2022

next.condition: able to sit: walked to the waiting room

evidence.note: Author's general knowledge of Ontario hospital infection screening at triage, active screening during 2020-2022.

steps.name: Move an ambulatory patient to the waiting room
steps.description: For a low-acuity patient who can sit, the paramedic walks the patient to a waiting room chair near the triage desk and the triage nurse accepts responsibility for monitoring. The stretcher is freed without waiting for a bed.

evidence.note: OAG 2023 describes the Peel Fit2Sit program (from October 2020) with offloads of about nine minutes for eligible patients; the 10% share of ambulance patients who can sit is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Quick-register the ambulance patient
steps.description: The unit clerk creates the emergency visit in the hospital system from the patient's name, date of birth and health card number read off the call report or wallet, so that orders and the triage note can be attached. Full registration with health card validation happens later at the bedside.

error.defect_description: Wrong patient picked from the master patient index or a duplicate chart created.

evidence.note: Author's general knowledge of ED quick registration; minutes estimated.

steps.name: Look for a free stretcher and nurse
steps.description: The charge nurse checks the tracking board for an empty, cleaned stretcher in the right zone and a nurse with room in their assignment, and asks the bed flow team whether admitted patients are about to leave. If nothing is free, the patient stays on the paramedics' stretcher.

evidence.note: OAG 2023 names the two main causes of offload delay: no nurse free to triage and take the patient, and no assessment room space. The 55% delayed share is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Wait on the paramedic stretcher for a space
steps.description: The patient lies on the ambulance stretcher in the offload hallway while the two paramedics stay with them, repeat vital signs and report changes to the triage nurse. The ambulance is out of service for 911 calls for the whole wait. Time here is the offload delay the paramedic service counts.

next.condition: dedicated offload nurse on duty takes the patient
a stretcher and nurse come free
delay long and several crews waiting: escalate

evidence.note: OAG 2023: 30 minutes is industry best practice, not met consistently, delays up to three hours elsewhere; Halton time at hospital was the third-highest of Ontario services benchmarked by ORH and rose from 2021 to 2022 (halton_pmp). Wait range is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Offload nurse assumes care in the offload area
steps.description: A nurse funded by the Dedicated Offload Nurse Program takes report, moves the patient onto a hospital stretcher in the offload area and monitors several ambulance patients at once, so the crew can leave before a treatment space opens. Coverage is limited to the hours the funding pays for.
outputs: patient under hospital care in offload area

evidence.note: Dedicated Offload Nurse Program since 2008, funded through municipalities (OAG 2023); offload times stay long even with an offload nurse. Share of delayed patients taken by an offload nurse is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Escalate a long offload delay
steps.description: The charge nurse calls the patient care manager or administrator on call and the paramedic superintendent, moves admitted patients waiting for beds into hallway spaces, opens over-capacity stretchers and asks inpatient units to pull admitted patients up. The action is logged on the board.

control.basis: Hospital overcapacity and ambulance offload escalation protocol agreed with the regional paramedic service

evidence.note: Author's general knowledge of hospital overcapacity escalation; frequency and minutes estimated.

steps.name: Reassess a patient waiting on the stretcher
steps.description: The triage nurse repeats the vital signs the paramedic reports as changed, re-checks the CTAS level and decides whether the patient must jump the queue for the next space or into the resuscitation bay.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of re-triage while waiting.

steps.name: Assign a stretcher and a primary nurse
steps.description: The charge nurse assigns the free space and a primary nurse on the tracking board and tells the paramedics where to take the patient. Sicker patients get the monitored acute spaces.

evidence.note: Author's general knowledge; minutes estimated.

steps.name: Prepare the treatment space
steps.description: The patient care assistant strips and wipes the stretcher if cleaning has not been done, puts on clean linen, checks the monitor and oxygen at the space and brings a gown, while the charge nurse finishes the assignment.

evidence.note: Author's estimate; cleaning between ED patients is often done by assistants or environmental services.

steps.name: Move patient and give bedside handover
steps.description: The paramedics wheel the patient to the space, slide them onto the hospital stretcher with the primary nurse and repeat the report. The nurse checks the identity band, takes a first set of vitals and looks for gaps in the medication and allergy history.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Sign the transfer of care
steps.description: The receiving nurse signs or is named on the paramedics' call report, and the transfer-of-care time is recorded. From this moment the hospital is responsible for the patient and the offload interval ends.
outputs: transfer of care time and receiving nurse recorded

control.basis: Ontario Ministry of Health ambulance documentation standards: call report records the time of transfer of care and the receiving clinician

evidence.note: Author's general knowledge of Ontario ambulance call report practice; the documentation standard was not opened.

steps.name: Complete the call report and clear the hospital
steps.description: The paramedics finish and upload the electronic call report, strip, wipe and remake their stretcher, restock supplies from the hospital cart and tell the ambulance communications centre they are available again.

evidence.note: Time at hospital includes post-transfer work and is a planning input for Halton Paramedic Services (halton_pmp); minutes are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Record the offload on the tracking board
steps.description: The unit clerk confirms the arrival and transfer-of-care times on the tracking board, which feed the hospital's offload report to the paramedic service and the Ontario Health ambulance offload indicator.

control.basis: Ontario Health Pay-for-Results program: ambulance offload time indicator

evidence.note: Ambulance offload time is one of six Pay-for-Results indicators Ontario Health ranks hospitals on (OAG 2023 section 4.6); clerk minutes estimated.

exceptions.name: Critical patient patched ahead
exceptions.description: The crew bypasses ambulance triage and hands over in the resuscitation bay.

exceptions.name: Offload delay
exceptions.description: No stretcher or nurse is free and the patient waits on the ambulance stretcher with the crew.

exceptions.name: Escalation for long delays
exceptions.description: Several crews are held and the charge nurse escalates to management and opens over-capacity spaces.

exceptions.name: Ambulatory patient to waiting room
exceptions.description: A low-acuity patient who can sit is walked to the waiting room and the crew leaves quickly.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from ambulance arrival to the crew clearing the hospital (about 60 and 150 minutes)

evidence.note: Author's estimate built from OAG 2023 (30-minute offload best practice not met consistently; delays up to three hours elsewhere) and halton_pmp (Halton time at hospital third-highest of benchmarked Ontario services, rising 2021-2022), plus about 15 minutes of paramedic post-transfer work. No Halton offload percentiles for 2019-2022 could be opened.

benchmarks.unit: minutes from arrival to transfer of care
benchmarks.population: Ontario paramedic services (industry best practice; no provincial target)

evidence.note: OAG 2023 section 4.3.3.

benchmarks.unit: minutes from arrival to transfer of care
benchmarks.population: Peel Regional Paramedic Services and William Osler Health System, low-acuity patients able to sit, from October 2020

evidence.note: OAG 2023 section 4.3.3.

pain_points.description: Paramedics wait with patients because no stretcher or nurse is free; the main causes are nurse availability and assessment space, often because admitted patients occupy ED stretchers.

evidence.note: OAG 2023 section 4.3.3.

pain_points.description: Offload nurse funding covers only part of the day, so long offloads continue even where the program exists.

evidence.note: OAG 2023: offload times remained long even at hospitals with a dedicated offload nurse.

pain_points.description: Ambulance patients join the same triage queue as walk-ins, so the crew waits for the triage nurse before handover even when a space is free.

evidence.note: OAG 2023: patients arriving by ambulance did not get priority over walk-ins.

assumptions: The simulated median time at hospital (about 72 minutes) is about 1.2 times the estimated 60-minute benchmark; it is kept because Halton time at hospital was among the highest of benchmarked Ontario services (halton_pmp), and both figures are estimates.
The process ends when the crew clears the hospital, so the simulated cycle time is the ambulance's time at hospital; the offload interval the province measures ends earlier, at step s17.
Step times describe the large site; ED space use is booked against the large site's treatment spaces (ed_spaces_otmh) as the representative site.
The ambulance crew resource is added because the crew and vehicle are what offload delay ties up; the count of 25 staffed ambulances on the road at peak in the region is the author's estimate.
Triage of ambulance patients (CTAS) is done inside this process; the triage workflow (hosp-ed-patient-triage) picks ambulance patients up at bedside registration.

The two paramedic steps with people = 2 count paramedic time in the simulated hands-on hours, which roughly doubles the FTE implied by touch time compared with hospital staff alone; stated FTE covers hospital roles only.
Hospital staffing FTE includes idle triage-desk time between arrivals, so stated FTE exceeds hospital hands-on time.
